options.text: Decompose fundraising into its constituent functions so each strand can be examined in turn.
options.verdict: Functional decomposition needs a function whose boundaries are known, and the chief executive cannot yet name the strands.

options.text: Run a SWOT so the internal and external pressures on fundraising are separated from the outset.
options.verdict: SWOT imposes a four-way classification on material that has not been surfaced, and the chief executive would be sorting before she has recalled.

options.text: Bring the capability model forward and use the session to grade fundraising capabilities for performance.
options.verdict: Grading capabilities requires knowing which ones are in play, which is the question the session is meant to open.

trap: Accepting a quality expressed as an adjective
stem: A tender response is due in a fortnight for a public-facing permit portal. The requirements set states that the portal must be fast, highly available, secure and easy to use. The sponsor considers these self-evident and does not want the tender delayed by what he calls wordsmithing. Vendors will price and design against whatever is issued.
why: Fast, available, secure and easy to use are aspirations until they carry numbers and conditions: response time at what percentile under what load, availability over what window excluding what, secure against which standard, usable measured how. Vendors will price against the loosest reading, and the organisation will have no basis to reject what arrives. The qualities also drive architecture, so leaving them vague concedes the design as well as the price.

options.text: Issue the tender as drafted and clarify the qualities during evaluation, when vendors can be questioned directly.
options.verdict: By evaluation the vendors have priced and designed against their own readings, and there is no agreed basis to compare them.

options.text: Add the qualities to the evaluation criteria with weightings, so vendors offering more are scored higher.
options.verdict: Scoring undefined qualities produces an assessment of the persuasiveness of the response rather than of the solution.

options.text: Move the qualities into the contract as service levels to be negotiated after the supplier is selected.
options.verdict: Negotiating service levels after selection removes the competitive pressure that would have made them affordable.

options.text: Specify each quality measurably, with load, percentile, availability window and standard, before the tender is issued.
options.verdict: Correct. A non-functional requirement without a measure cannot be priced, designed against or accepted.

trap: Believing the documented procedure over the work as performed
stem: A manufacturer's quality procedure requires a four-step inspection at the end of each shift. Supervisors confirm in interview that it is followed. The system records inspection completion at a median of forty seconds, which the analyst calculates is too short for four steps. Defect escapes have risen 40% in a year. A new shift roster started in March.
why: Three sources disagree: the procedure says four steps, the supervisors say it is followed, and the timing data says it cannot be. Asking again produces the same answer, because the supervisors are describing the procedure they are accountable for rather than knowingly misleading. Watching the inspection performed is the only way to establish what actually happens, which is exactly the gap between stated and actual practice that observation exists to close.

options.text: Re-interview the supervisors with the timing data in front of them, so the discrepancy has to be addressed directly.
options.verdict: Confronting people with data that implies non-compliance produces defensiveness, and they may sincerely believe the procedure is followed.

options.text: Observe the inspection being performed across several shifts to establish what is actually done.
options.verdict: Correct. Where stated practice and system evidence conflict, watching the work is the technique that resolves it.

options.text: Analyse the defect data to determine which of the four steps is failing to catch the escapes.
options.verdict: This assumes all four steps are being performed, which is the assumption the timing data has put in doubt.

options.text: Review the procedure against the new shift roster, since the rise in escapes coincides with the March change.
options.verdict: The roster is worth noting but the forty-second median is the sharper signal, and it points at what is done rather than when.

trap: Planning engagement when the problem is that authority is unlocated
stem: Three requirements decisions have now stalled for over a month each. In every case two directors each believed the other was accountable, and in one case a third area turned out to hold the mandate following a restructure eighteen months ago that was never documented. The programme sponsor asks the analyst to improve stakeholder engagement so decisions move faster.
why: Engagement planning decides how often and how formally to deal with people whose roles are known. Here nobody can say where the decision rights sit, because a restructure moved them and was never recorded. Organisational modelling maps the units, roles, reporting lines and, critically, where responsibility actually rests, which is the input the governance plan needs before any engagement approach can be designed around it.

options.text: Build a stakeholder map positioning each director by influence and interest, then set engagement accordingly.
options.verdict: Influence and interest describe attitude and power, not who holds the mandate, which is the specific thing nobody can establish.

options.text: Escalate each stalled decision to the sponsor, who can direct which director decides in each case.
options.verdict: It unblocks three decisions by substituting the sponsor's authority and leaves the fourth to stall the same way.

options.text: Model the organisation's units, roles and reporting lines to locate where responsibility for each decision now sits.
options.verdict: Correct. Undocumented movement of decision rights is a structural question, and the model has to precede the governance plan.

options.text: Document the decision-making approach in the governance plan, naming an approver for each requirement type.
options.verdict: Naming approvers is the right output but cannot be done credibly until the analyst knows who actually holds the mandate.

trap: Applying a value basis where the basis is imposed from outside
stem: A superannuation fund must implement a legislative change by 1 July or face penalty and licence conditions. The same release carries a member portal redesign with a strong benefit case and a data quality fix that the legislative change depends on. The product owner proposes ranking all three on business value, which places the portal redesign first.
why: Value is one basis for prioritisation among several, and it is the wrong one where a regulatory deadline and a dependency are in play. The legislative change is not competing for a place; it has a date attached and a consequence for missing it. The data quality fix must precede it regardless of its own value. Prioritisation on value alone is exactly how a fund misses a statutory date while delivering a well-liked portal.

options.text: Sequence on the binding constraints first, dependency then regulatory date, and rank the portal redesign on value within what remains.
options.verdict: Correct. Prioritisation bases include dependency and regulatory deadline, and those govern before value is consulted.

options.text: Rank all three on business value as proposed, since a consistent basis is what makes a ranking defensible.
options.verdict: Consistency applied to the wrong basis produces a defensible route to a licence condition.

options.text: Split the release so the legislative change is delivered separately and the other two ranked on value between them.
options.verdict: This isolates the legislative item but strands the data quality fix it depends on in the value-ranked release.

options.text: Escalate to the executive, since a decision with licence consequences is above the product owner's authority.
options.verdict: The sequencing follows from the constraints and needs no ruling; escalating a soluble prioritisation question delays it.

trap: Analysing a process that has never been depicted
stem: A council's development approval times have doubled since a new case system went live. Four teams touch each application and each describes its own part differently; no end-to-end depiction exists. The service manager has asked the analyst to identify the waste and delay in the process so the bottleneck can be removed before the next reporting period.
why: Analysis presupposes a depiction: waste, delay, variation and rework are identified against a model of the flow, and with four teams describing only their own parts there is nothing to analyse across. The sequence is to model the end-to-end process first, then analyse it. Going straight to bottleneck-hunting produces four local opinions about which other team is the problem, which is the state the council is already in.

options.text: Interview each of the four teams about where they experience delay and consolidate the responses into findings.
options.verdict: Four local views of delay is what the council already has, and consolidating them does not create the end-to-end picture.

options.text: Compare approval times against the previous system to isolate which stage the new system slowed.
options.verdict: Comparison at the aggregate level shows that it slowed, not where, because the stages have never been defined consistently.

options.text: Measure cycle time at each team boundary so the bottleneck can be identified from the data alone.
options.verdict: Boundary timings need agreed boundaries, and the four teams do not currently describe the process in compatible terms.

options.text: Model the end-to-end process across the four teams first, then analyse it for waste, delay and rework.
options.verdict: Correct. You cannot analyse a process that has not been depicted, and the inconsistent local accounts are the reason.

trap: Choosing the notation that suits the reader rather than the subject
stem: An analyst must specify how a returned parcel is handled. Six parties are involved: the customer, the courier, two warehouse teams, finance and a third-party refurbisher, and the difficulty is the hand-offs between them and what happens when one party rejects the parcel. A developer has asked for use cases because that is what the team builds from.
why: The substance here is a chain of hand-offs between six parties, with branching where a party rejects. That is business work flowing between actors, which is what a process model expresses. A use case describes one actor pursuing a goal through the solution and would fragment a six-party chain into disconnected pieces, losing precisely the hand-offs that are the problem. What the team prefers to build from does not change what the subject is.

options.text: Write use cases as the developer asks, since specifications the team cannot build from have no practical value.
options.verdict: The team's preference is worth serving, but not by choosing a notation that cannot express the hand-offs at issue.

options.text: Model the end-to-end process with the six parties and the rejection branches, then derive use cases where the actor interacts with the solution.
options.verdict: Correct. Model the flow in the notation that carries it, then supply the interaction detail the team needs.

options.text: Produce a sequence diagram, since the ordering of exchanges between the six parties is the essential content.
options.verdict: Sequence diagrams order messages between components; these are business parties performing work, not systems exchanging messages.

options.text: Write user stories for each party's part in the return so the work can be sized and scheduled.
options.verdict: Stories deliberately defer detail and would leave the hand-off and rejection logic unspecified, which is the entire difficulty.

trap: Letting an elicitation device become the delivered solution
stem: A clickable prototype built to elicit requirements for a claims intake screen has been well received. The sponsor now proposes that the delivery team extend the prototype into the production solution, since stakeholders have already agreed it and rebuilding would waste the work. The prototype was built in a rapid tool with no error handling, no security model and no test coverage.
why: The prototype did its job: it made an abstract requirement concrete and got agreement. What it is not is a solution, having none of the error handling, security or test coverage production requires, and the decision being proposed converts a throwaway artefact into an evolutionary one after the fact. The analyst should preserve what the prototype established, which is the agreed interaction, and be clear that the artefact itself is not the deliverable.

options.text: Specify the requirements the prototype established, and let the team build against them rather than extending the prototype.
options.verdict: Correct. The prototype's value is the agreement it produced, which transfers; its construction does not.

options.text: Extend the prototype as the sponsor proposes, adding error handling, security and tests as the first work items.
options.verdict: This retrofits into a rapid-tool artefact the very qualities its construction traded away, usually at more cost than rebuilding.

options.text: Ask the delivery team to assess whether the prototype tool is suitable for production and be guided by their answer.
options.verdict: It defers a decision the analyst can already inform, and frames a requirements question as a tooling one.

options.text: Rebuild the prototype to production standards in the same tool so stakeholders see no change in what they agreed.
options.verdict: Stakeholders agreed to the interaction, not to the implementation, so preserving the tool for their comfort constrains the build for no benefit.

trap: Confusing whether a requirement is well written with whether it is worth having
stem: A requirements set has passed a review in which testers confirmed every item was unambiguous, atomic, testable and consistently worded. Two weeks later the business sponsor reads the set and says that a third of it describes work her area no longer does following a service redesign. The reviewers were the same testers who will write the test cases.
why: The review verified the requirements, establishing that they are well formed, and it did so correctly. It did not validate them, which asks whether they deliver value to the business and align with its needs, and it could not, because the participants were testers rather than the people who know the service redesign. The same technique serves both purposes, so what matters is who reviews and against what question.

options.text: Re-run the review with a stricter quality checklist so that obsolete requirements are caught in future.
options.verdict: No quality checklist would catch this: the obsolete items are well written, which is why they passed.

options.text: Accept the outcome, since verification is the analyst's accountability and validation belongs to the sponsor.
options.verdict: Validating requirements is a business analysis task, and it is the analyst who must convene it with the right participants.

options.text: Convene a validation review with the business stakeholders, examining whether each requirement still delivers value.
options.verdict: Correct. Verification asked whether the requirements were well written; validation asks whether they are the right ones.

options.text: Trace each requirement to a business objective, which will expose the third that no longer supports one.
options.verdict: Tracing would expose them, but the objectives themselves moved in the redesign, so the business still has to confirm the set.

trap: Treating mitigation as though it removed the risk
stem: A retailer's change strategy carries a risk that a single supplier of a payment component fails during peak trading. The team has added monitoring and an escalation path, and the risk has been closed in the register on the basis that it is now mitigated. Peak trading begins in eleven weeks and no alternative supplier has been identified.
why: Monitoring and escalation detect the failure sooner and shorten the response; they do not reduce the likelihood that the supplier fails, nor the impact if it does during peak. What remains after a response is applied is residual risk, and it has to be assessed and either accepted explicitly or addressed by a response that changes the exposure, such as transfer or a second supplier. Closing the risk records a decision nobody made.

options.text: Accept the closure, since monitoring and escalation are proportionate responses and the register reflects the team's judgement.
options.verdict: The responses are reasonable but they act on detection, not on likelihood or impact, so the exposure is unchanged.

options.text: Raise the risk again at a higher severity so that the executive is obliged to fund a second supplier.
options.verdict: Inflating severity to force an outcome corrupts the register and substitutes manipulation for analysis.

options.text: Move the item to the issues log, since supplier concentration is a present condition rather than a future event.
options.verdict: Concentration is a present condition but the failure is an uncertain future event, which keeps it a risk.

options.text: Reopen it with the residual exposure assessed, and put the remaining response options to the decision-maker for an explicit choice.
options.verdict: Correct. Mitigation changes a risk rather than closing it, and accepting what remains has to be a decision on the record.

trap: Mapping where people sit when the question is what they may do
stem: An audit has found that in a grants system some officers can both create a payment and approve it. The finance controller has asked the analyst to establish the extent of the problem across all roles and objects before the remediation is scoped. An organisation chart is available and current. Eleven roles and nine object types exist in the system.
why: The audit finding concerns what each role is permitted to do to each object, and separation of duties is only visible when create, approve, amend and delete are laid out role by role and object by object. An organisation chart shows where people sit and answers a different question entirely. The matrix makes gaps, overlaps and the specific create-and-approve breach countable across all ninety-nine combinations rather than anecdotal.

options.text: Model the organisation so the reporting lines show which officers should not hold both permissions.
options.verdict: Reporting lines describe position rather than permission, and a separation-of-duties breach is defined by the permissions.

options.text: Build a matrix of the eleven roles against the nine object types and the actions permitted on each.
options.verdict: Correct. Permission by role and object is what exposes overlaps, gaps and separation-of-duties breaches systematically.

options.text: Specify a business rule that no officer may approve a payment they created, and pass it to the delivery team.
options.verdict: The rule is right but scoping remediation needs the extent first, and the audit asked about all roles rather than this one breach.

options.text: Extract the current access list from the system and review it with each role owner for correctness.
options.verdict: The list shows who currently holds what, which conflates the assignment with the permission design the audit is questioning.

trap: Treating a recurring symptom with a fourth fix
stem: A billing system has produced duplicate invoices three times in eighteen months. Each occurrence was traced to a different batch job and each was patched. The third occurrence affected 4,000 customers. The vendor has proposed a fourth patch and a monitoring alert. The finance director has asked the analyst whether to accept it.
why: Three different batch jobs producing the same failure mode points past any of the three to a condition they share, in scheduling, in restart handling or in the absence of an idempotency control. Patching the third job removes the third symptom and leaves whatever produced all three intact, which is why the pattern has already survived two fixes. The alert would detect the fourth occurrence rather than prevent it.

options.text: Trace the three occurrences back to the condition they have in common before accepting any further patch.
options.verdict: Correct. A failure mode surviving two fixes in three different places is the signature of a shared cause.

options.text: Accept the patch and the alert, since the alert will catch any recurrence before customers are affected.
options.verdict: Detection after the fact is not prevention, and 4,000 customers were affected before anyone noticed last time.

options.text: Escalate to the vendor's account management, since three failures in eighteen months indicates a quality problem on their side.
options.verdict: Contract pressure may be warranted but it does not identify the cause, and the fourth occurrence would arrive regardless.

options.text: Assess the enterprise limitations around batch scheduling, since the failures all originate in scheduled processing.
options.verdict: Closer, but it assumes the cause is environmental before the three occurrences have been traced to anything in common.

trap: Estimating and building before the boundary has been drawn
stem: A programme to modernise a licensing service has absorbed adjacent work three times: first inspections, then a public register, then complaints handling. Each absorption was agreed informally in a meeting. The sponsor now wants a firm estimate and delivery date. Nobody can produce a current statement of what is in and out of scope.
why: An estimate is a function of scope, and this scope has expanded three times without ever being stated, so any figure produced now would be an estimate of something undefined and would be absorbed again within weeks. Scope modelling draws the boundary explicitly, including what sits just outside it, which is what makes further absorption a visible decision rather than a meeting-room agreement.

options.text: Estimate the four workstreams separately so the sponsor has a figure for each of the absorbed areas.
options.verdict: Four estimates against four undefined areas inherit the same problem, and nothing prevents a fifth absorption.

options.text: Ask the sponsor to freeze scope at its current extent so the estimate can be produced against a stable base.
options.verdict: Freezing an unstated scope freezes an ambiguity; nobody could say afterwards what had been frozen.

options.text: Model the scope boundary explicitly, stating what is in, what is out and what sits adjacent, then estimate against it.
options.verdict: Correct. The boundary has to exist before it can be estimated or defended, and naming the adjacent work makes further absorption explicit.

options.text: Trace the three absorbed areas back to the programme's business objectives to test whether they belong.
options.verdict: A reasonable test of each absorption, but it evaluates past decisions rather than producing the boundary the estimate needs.

trap: Reaching for a workflow notation when the exchange between components is the requirement
stem: An intermittent failure occurs when a payment authorisation, a fraud check and a ledger posting are triggered by the same transaction. It appears only under load and always involves the ledger recording a posting before the fraud service has replied. Four components are involved. The business process model shows the activities and has not helped.
why: The activities are known; what is not specified is the order and timing of the messages between the four components, including which calls block and which return asynchronously. A process model shows business activities and cannot express that, which is why it has not helped. Sequence diagrams order the exchanges along a time axis, which is where a race between a reply and a posting becomes visible.

options.text: Model the process again in more detail, adding the system steps beneath each business activity.
options.verdict: More detail in a notation that has no time axis still cannot show that the posting precedes the reply.

options.text: Produce a state model of the transaction so the permitted transitions between statuses are defined.
options.verdict: State modelling would constrain what the transaction may become, but the fault is in the ordering of messages, not the statuses.

options.text: Specify non-functional requirements for response time under load, since the failure only appears when the system is busy.
options.verdict: Load exposes the defect but does not cause it; a faster fraud service would hide an ordering fault rather than fix it.

options.text: Diagram the ordered exchange of messages between the four components, showing which calls block and which do not.
options.verdict: Correct. Ordering of messages between components over time is what sequence diagrams express.

trap: Designing for an average user who does not exist
stem: A government service is being redesigned for 200,000 annual users. Design decisions keep being justified by reference to the typical user, but the cohort includes people using assistive technology, people with no reliable internet access, agents acting on behalf of others, and a high-volume professional group. The team has a complete stakeholder list and an engagement plan.
why: The list establishes who the stakeholders are and the plan establishes how they will be dealt with; neither captures that four groups have materially different needs, contexts and constraints. Personas characterise those groups so design decisions can be tested against each rather than against an average that describes none of them. The typical user in this cohort is a composite that no actual user resembles.

options.text: Segment the 200,000 users by volume and design for the largest segment, since it represents the majority of transactions.
options.verdict: Volume weighting is how the assistive technology and low-connectivity groups get designed out, and they are the ones with least alternative.

options.text: Develop personas for the distinct user groups so design decisions can be tested against each set of needs and constraints.
options.verdict: Correct. Personas exist precisely because a cohort with materially different needs cannot be served by an average.

options.text: Add the four groups to the stakeholder map, positioned by influence and interest, and engage them accordingly.
options.verdict: Influence and interest govern engagement; they do not describe the needs and constraints that design decisions must satisfy.

options.text: Run usability testing with a representative sample once the design is complete, and remediate what it finds.
options.verdict: Testing at the end finds what the design already excluded, when changing it is most expensive.

trap: Describing the work when the rules are about what the object may become
stem: A tribunal case may be lodged, allocated, listed, adjourned, reserved, determined, withdrawn or struck out. Disputes have arisen because a case was reinstated after being struck out, and because one was adjourned after determination. The registrar wants the rules about what may follow what specified unambiguously. A process model of case handling already exists and is accurate.
why: The existing process model correctly describes what registry staff do, and it is not the artefact in question. What the registrar needs is which statuses a case may move to from each current status, and under what event or condition, so that adjourning a determined case is prevented by specification rather than by staff diligence. That is a state model, and its transitions are exactly the disputed rules.

options.text: Extend the process model with decision points showing where each status change is made.
options.verdict: Decision points show where staff act but not which transitions are permissible, which is what the two disputes turned on.

options.text: Specify business rules describing the conditions under which each status change is allowed.
options.verdict: Closer, but a list of rules over eight statuses obscures the completeness question a transition model makes visible.

options.text: Write use cases for reinstatement and adjournment so the two disputed interactions are fully specified.
options.verdict: This specifies the two known disputes and leaves the remaining transitions unstated, so the next dispute is simply a different pair.

options.text: Model the states a case may occupy and the permitted transitions between them, with the event or condition for each.
options.verdict: Correct. What an object may become, from where and on what event, is what state modelling specifies.

trap: Reading a self-selected sample as though it were representative
stem: A satisfaction survey issued after a portal launch returned 310 responses from 12,000 users, a 2.6% response rate, and reports 82% satisfaction. The sponsor wants to publish it as evidence the launch succeeded. Support ticket volume has tripled since go-live, and the survey was linked from a banner on the portal's home page.
why: A 2.6% response rate from a banner on the portal reaches people who reached the portal, used it and chose to respond, which selects for those it worked for. Users who abandoned it or went to the phone channel are structurally absent, and tripled ticket volume suggests there are many. The figure is not wrong as a description of the respondents; it simply cannot support a claim about the 12,000, and the sampling method is the reason.

options.text: Report the result with its response rate and sampling method, and measure performance from the channels the non-respondents used.
options.verdict: Correct. Disclose what the sample supports, and get the missing population from ticket and channel data.

options.text: Publish the 82% as the sponsor asks, noting the response rate in a footnote for transparency.
options.verdict: A footnote does not repair a sample drawn from the successful users, and the headline would still assert what it cannot support.

options.text: Reissue the survey by email to all 12,000 users to raise the response rate to a credible level.
options.verdict: Email raises the rate but still selects for people willing to respond, and does nothing about the tripled tickets already available as evidence.

options.text: Discard the survey result, since a 2.6% response rate carries no information about solution performance.
options.verdict: It carries real information about the respondents; the error is generalising it, not collecting it.

trap: Confusing an internal shortcoming with an external threat
stem: An analyst is reviewing a draft SWOT prepared by a regional airline's strategy team before it goes to the board. Four of the entries are shown below. The chief executive has said the analysis feels right and does not want it over-engineered. The airline's fleet renewal decision is due next quarter.

exhibit.title: Draft SWOT entries under review
rows: Ageing fleet with high maintenance cost
exhibit.note: Strengths and weaknesses are internal; opportunities and threats are external.

why: Three of the four entries are on the wrong axis. Lacking a booking capability and owning an ageing fleet are both internal, which makes them weaknesses; a competitor launching routes is external, which makes it a threat. Only the brand entry is correctly placed. The distinction matters because weaknesses are what the airline can act on directly and threats are what it must respond to, and misplacing them sends the board's fleet decision the wrong signal about what is within its control.

options.text: Leave the placements, since the board is concerned with the substance of each item rather than its quadrant.
options.verdict: The quadrant is the substance: it states whether the airline can act on the item or must respond to it.

options.text: Move the capability gap and the ageing fleet to weaknesses, and the competitor's route launch to threats.
options.verdict: Correct. Internal attributes are strengths or weaknesses; external events are opportunities or threats.

options.text: Merge the ageing fleet and the capability gap into a single entry, since both concern investment the airline has deferred.
options.verdict: Merging distinct items to explain a shared cause loses two separate positions the board must act on, and still leaves them misplaced.

options.text: Replace the SWOT with a capability analysis, which would classify the fleet and booking items without the axis problem.
options.verdict: Capability analysis is a useful companion but discards the external scan the board needs alongside its fleet decision.

trap: Specifying the happy path and calling the requirement complete
stem: Requirements for an online renewal transaction have been signed off. Each describes what happens when the customer supplies valid details and payment succeeds. In testing, the team finds no specification for an expired card, a part-completed renewal resumed the next day, a customer whose licence is under suspension, or a payment that times out after debiting.
why: Every gap found in testing is an alternate or exception flow, and it is the presence of those flows that distinguishes a use case from a description of the successful path. A use case specifies the main flow, the alternatives and the exceptions together, which forces the analyst to ask what else can happen at each step. Signing off only the successful path defers all four questions to whoever is writing the code.

options.text: Raise four change requests so the missing conditions are added through the agreed change process.
options.verdict: These are not changes to agreed requirements; they are parts of the requirement that were never specified.

options.text: Add acceptance criteria covering the four conditions to the requirements already signed off.
options.verdict: Criteria could record the expected outcomes but not the flows that reach them, and four is unlikely to be all of them.

options.text: Ask the test team to define the expected behaviour, since they identified the gaps and understand the conditions.
options.verdict: This delegates a specification decision to testers, who would be validating their own assumptions afterwards.

options.text: Specify each transaction as a use case with its main flow, alternate flows and exceptions, and validate the complete set.
options.verdict: Correct. Alternate and exception flows are part of the use case, not an addition discovered during testing.

trap: Writing a system instruction and calling it a user story
stem: A backlog contains items in the form as a user I want the record saved to the audit table so that the record is saved to the audit table. The team cannot prioritise them because nobody can say who benefits or by how much. The delivery lead argues the format is correct because each begins with as a user I want and the team agreed the template.
why: The template is being satisfied while the content it exists to carry is absent: as a user names no actual role, and the benefit clause restates the action rather than stating what it is worth to anyone. Prioritisation needs value, and these items carry none, which is why the team is stuck. A user story is a placeholder for a conversation, and these have no one to have it with.

options.text: Prioritise on technical dependency instead, since the items describe system behaviour rather than user-facing value.
options.verdict: Dependency sequences work but never establishes whether it is worth doing, which is what the team cannot currently answer.

options.text: Convert them to non-functional requirements, since auditability is a quality of the solution rather than a user need.
options.verdict: Some may be, but the underlying problem is that no role or value has been identified, which the conversion does not supply.

options.text: Rewrite them with the actual role and the value to that role, going back to the stakeholders where neither is known.
options.verdict: Correct. Without a real role and a genuine benefit there is nothing to prioritise, and the conversation is the point of the story.

options.text: Accept them as written and size them by effort, letting the team schedule by cost until value becomes clearer.
options.verdict: Sequencing by cost alone optimises for cheapness and would deliver low-value items first on principle.

task: 7.6 Analyze Potential Value and Recommend Solution
trap: Assessing the product and forgetting the supplier behind it
stem: A council has scored three products against its evaluation criteria. The highest scorer is supplied by a two-year-old firm of nine people, currently loss-making, whose product is genuinely the best fit and whose reference site is a council half the size. The contract would run seven years and the product would hold the rates register.
why: Evaluation criteria judge the product and this one judged it correctly. What has not been assessed is whether the supplier can sustain a seven-year commitment holding a critical register: financial viability, capacity relative to a council twice the size of its only reference, and what happens to the rates data if the firm fails. That is vendor assessment, and it is a separate question from product fit rather than a lower-weighted criterion within it.

options.text: Award to the highest scorer, since the criteria were agreed in advance and departing from them would be indefensible.
options.verdict: The criteria assessed the product; awarding on them alone means the supplier was never assessed at all.

options.text: Re-score with financial viability added as a weighted criterion so the position is reflected in the totals.
options.verdict: Folding viability into a product score lets a strong functional fit outweigh a supplier that may not survive the term.

options.text: Award to the second-placed product, since a seven-year contract over the rates register cannot carry supplier risk.
options.verdict: This discards the best-fitting product before establishing whether the risk can be addressed through escrow, guarantees or contract terms.

options.text: Assess the supplier separately on viability, capacity and continuity, and put both assessments to the decision-maker.
options.verdict: Correct. Product fit and supplier capability are distinct judgements and both belong in front of the decision-maker.

trap: Calling a meeting a workshop and expecting a work product from it
stem: Three sessions described as requirements workshops have produced no agreed output. Each ran without a stated objective, without a facilitator, with attendance varying week to week, and with notes taken by whoever remembered. Participants say the sessions are useful discussions. The programme needs a confirmed set of elicitation results before analysis can proceed.
why: What has been running is a series of meetings. A workshop is defined by having a stated output, a facilitator who is neutral on the content, the participants with authority to agree that output, and someone recording decisions. All four are absent, which is precisely why three sessions produced useful discussion and nothing confirmable. Adding a fourth session in the same form produces a fourth discussion.

options.text: Circulate the accumulated notes for written confirmation, which obtains agreement without another session.
options.verdict: The notes are of unknown provenance from varying attendees, so confirming them would baseline whatever happened to be written down.

options.text: Run the next session with a defined output, a facilitator, the participants who can agree it, and a scribe.
options.verdict: Correct. Those four elements are what make a session a workshop rather than a discussion.

options.text: Replace the sessions with individual interviews, since the group format has failed three times.
options.verdict: The format has not been tried yet, and interviews cannot produce agreement between parties who need to agree with each other.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to mandate attendance, since varying participation is the most visible of the four problems.
options.verdict: Consistent attendance at a session with no objective, facilitator or scribe still produces a discussion.
